content: An octahedron is a polyhedron characterized by having eight faces. A regular octahedron is a type of Platonic solid, consisting of eight equilateral triangles, with four triangles meeting at each vertex. The symmetry group of the octahedron is denoted as Oh, which has an order of 48. Subgroups of this symmetry group include D3d (order 12), representing the symmetry of a triangular antiprism; D4h (order 16), corresponding to the symmetry of a square bipyramid; and Td (order 24), which is the symmetry group of a rectified tetrahedron. These symmetries can be highlighted by various decorations applied to the faces. The octahedron is also classified as a three-dimensional cross polytope. In Cartesian coordinates, an octahedron can be positioned with its center at the origin and its vertices aligned along the coordinate axes. The vertices' Cartesian coordinates are determined accordingly. The surface area (A) and volume (V) of a regular octahedron with edge length (a) are given by specific mathematical formulas. The volume of the octahedron is four times that of a regular tetrahedron with the same edge length, while its surface area is twice as large, as it has eight triangular faces compared to the tetrahedron's four. Geometrically, the interior of the compound formed by two dual tetrahedra is an octahedron. This compound, known as the stella octangula, represents the first and only stellation of the octahedron. The vertices of the octahedron are located at the midpoints of the edges of a tetrahedron, establishing a relationship between the two shapes. This relationship is analogous to how the cuboctahedron and icosidodecahedron relate to other Platonic solids. By dividing the edges of an octahedron in the ratio of the golden mean, one can define the vertices of an icosahedron. This process involves placing vectors along the edges of the octahedron such that each face is bounded by a cycle, and then partitioning each edge according to the golden mean along the direction of its vector. Five octahedra can define any given icosahedron in this manner, collectively forming a regular compound. Octahedra and tetrahedra can alternate to create a vertex-, edge-, and face-uniform tessellation of space, known as the octet truss, a concept introduced by Buckminster Fuller. This tessellation is unique among the Platonic solids, apart from the regular tessellation of cubes, and is one of the 28 convex uniform honeycombs. Another tessellation involves octahedra and cuboctahedra. The octahedron is unique among the Platonic solids in having an even number of faces meeting at each vertex. Consequently, it is the only member of this group to possess mirror planes that do not pass through any of its faces. Using the standard nomenclature for Johnson solids, the octahedron is referred to as a square bipyramid. The octahedron can also be considered a rectified tetrahedron, as demonstrated by a two-color face model. With this coloring, the octahedron exhibits tetrahedral symmetry. This relationship can be observed in the truncation sequence between a tetrahedron and its dual. In the physical world, the octahedron is commonly recognized as a d8 in role-playing games, one of the more frequently used polyhedral dice. If each edge of an octahedron is replaced by a one-ohm resistor, the electrical resistance between opposite vertices is 1/2 ohms, while the resistance between adjacent vertices is 5/12 ohms. Natural crystals such as diamond, alum, and fluorite often exhibit octahedral shapes. The regular octahedron has six vertices and twelve edges, which are the minimum for an octahedron. Non-regular octahedra, however, may have up to twelve vertices and eighteen edges.
